scenario: AITA for disagreeing with our HR? | I am a 7 month newly hired employee for a big corporation. Last night our HR sent out a five page memo to all employees titled "Office Discipline". Basically, they were reminding everyone of the various rules around the office. Like not loitering during office hours, sticking to our lunch schedules, the correct dress code, wearing of IDs at all times etc. In my 6 month stay here our HR hasn't issued me an office ID card. Despite their large number of employees (they have an entire floor to themselves unlike multiple departments in one floor), they are slow. They took about 5 months to process my payroll alone, so the delay in ID cards are not a surprise to us. Everyone without an office ID just started using government issued IDs to be able to enter our building but this morning, security started telling everyone that starting next week anyone without an ID will have their names be noted and be reported to HR. I promptly called HR when I got to my desk to ask for a status for my (and my other colleagues) ID. They told me that they can't print our IDs yet because the team in charge is swarmed with other "projects" and suggested that we can print our own IDs, and gave us the template. My colleagues and I disagreed with this. We argued that we don't want to make up for the short comings of HR, by shelling out money from our own pockets to print our IDs, and that it should have been provided to us in the first place. We plan on just keep using whatever IDs we have right now be damned whatever happens next week. So, AITA for disagreeing with our HR?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether disagreeing with HR in this situation is right or wrong. Let me start by understanding the scenario. I'm a 7-month newly hired employee at a big corporation. Last night, HR sent out a five-page memo titled "Office Discipline." They reminded everyone about various office rules, like not loitering during office hours, sticking to lunch schedules, dress code, and wearing IDs at all times. Now, in my 6 months here, HR hasn't issued me an office ID card. The company is big, with an entire floor to themselves, unlike multiple departments sharing one floor. Despite their size, they're slow. It took them about 5 months to process my payroll, so the delay in ID cards isn't a surprise. Everyone without an office ID started using government-issued IDs to enter the building. This morning, security announced that starting next week, anyone without an ID will have their names noted and reported to HR. I called HR when I got to my desk to ask about the status of my ID and my colleagues'. They said they can't print our IDs yet because the team in charge is swamped with other "projects" and suggested we print our own IDs using a template they provided. My colleagues and I disagreed with this. We argued that we don't want to make up for HR's shortcomings by spending our own money to print IDs, and that it should have been provided to us in the first place. We plan to just keep using whatever IDs we have right now, regardless of what happens next week. So, the question is: Is it right or wrong to disagree with HR in this situation? I need to figure out whether this is appropriate or not. First, I should consider the company's policies. The memo from HR clearly states that IDs are required. They reminded everyone about the rules, including wearing IDs at all times. So, according to the rules, we should have IDs. However, HR hasn't provided us with IDs despite being employed for several months. They're slow, and it's not the first time they've been delayed. They suggested we print our own IDs, but we refused because we don't want to spend our own money and believe it's HR's responsibility to provide them. On one hand, following company rules is important. If the policy requires an ID, we should comply. On the other hand, HR's failure to provide IDs in a timely manner is problematic. It's their responsibility to ensure that employees have the necessary IDs. Disagreeing with HR in this case seems justified because they're not fulfilling their obligations. However, it's also important to communicate our concerns constructively rather than just refusing to comply. Maybe we should escalate the issue or find a middle ground. Another consideration is the potential consequences of not having an ID. Security will start noting names and reporting to HR. This could lead to disciplinary actions against us, even though the root cause is HR's inefficiency. So, while it's understandable to be frustrated with HR's delays, it's also important to find a solution that complies with the company's policies. Perhaps we can request an extension or alternative arrangements until HR can provide the IDs. In summary, disagreeing with HR is justified due to their failure to provide necessary IDs, but it's also important to address the issue constructively to avoid potential consequences.
